A six-figure reference locates you to 100 metres, an eight-figure to 10 metres, a ten-figure to 1 metre. A romer — a small printed scale with tenths marked, usually on the corner of a compass baseplate — turns the estimate into a measurement. Two hard cautions. First, a grid reference is meaningless without its zone or square prefix, since the same six figures repeat in every 100-kilometre square on Earth; always give the letters. Second, coordinates are tied to a datum, and datum shifts are large enough to matter: a position on the old North American Datum of 1927 can plot more than two hundred metres from the same coordinates on WGS 84, and Britain's OSGB36 differs from WGS 84 by up to about a hundred metres. Set a satellite receiver to the datum printed in the map's collar, or accept an error larger than most navigational tolerances.

sections.heading: The Declination Diagram and the Three Norths
sections.body: Printed in the collar of nearly every topographic sheet is a small fan of arrows that quietly reconciles three incompatible definitions of north. Ignoring it introduces a systematic error into every bearing you take, and systematic errors do not average out. True north is the direction of the geographic North Pole, the axis about which the Earth spins. It is the reference for latitude and longitude and is fixed. Grid north is the direction of the vertical grid lines on the sheet. Because a flat grid cannot exactly cover a curved Earth, grid north diverges from true north everywhere except along a zone's central meridian, by an amount called convergence — typically under two degrees within a UTM zone but larger at high latitudes. Magnetic north is the direction a compass needle points, governed by the Earth's magnetic field, which is neither aligned with the axis nor stable. The angle between grid north and magnetic north is the grid magnetic angle, or magnetic declination when measured from true north. It varies enormously with position: at present it is roughly zero along a line running through the eastern United States, reaching around fifteen degrees west in the Pacific Northwest and similar magnitudes east in Maine, and exceeding thirty degrees in parts of Alaska and the high Arctic. It also varies with time. The north magnetic pole has migrated from Arctic Canada toward Siberia at accelerating rates, exceeding fifty kilometres a year in the 2000s and 2010s, which forced an unscheduled out-of-cycle update to the World Magnetic Model in early 2019. Annual change is typically a few minutes of arc per year, so a declination figure printed on a twenty-year-old sheet may be two to three degrees stale. Converting is where people go wrong, and it is worth having a phrase you trust rather than reasoning it out in the cold. If declination is west, magnetic bearings are numerically larger than grid bearings, so to go from the map to the compass you add, and from the compass to the map you subtract. If declination is east, reverse it. The old mnemonic "grid to mag, add" holds for a westerly declination only, which is why it is safest to read the diagram itself, which draws the arrows in their actual relative positions and states the angle and the annual change. The size of the error is worth internalising. A one-degree bearing error puts you about seventeen metres off per kilometre travelled; ten degrees puts you about a hundred and seventy-five metres off per kilometre. Over a five-kilometre leg in poor visibility, an uncorrected fifteen-degree declination places you more than a kilometre from your target — comfortably enough to miss a hut, a col, or a valley entirely. Many modern compasses have an adjustable declination screw that sets the correction once and removes the arithmetic from the field, which is strongly preferable to doing mental arithmetic while cold and tired.

sections.heading: National and Specialist Variations in the Symbol Set
sections.body: The phrase "standard topographic symbols" conceals a real diversity. The broad grammar — colour classes, contours, graded line weights — is shared worldwide, but the specific vocabulary differs by agency, and assuming otherwise is how experienced navigators embarrass themselves abroad. United States Geological Survey quadrangles, historically at 1:24,000 covering 7.5 minutes of latitude and longitude, use contour intervals in feet on older sheets and a green tint keyed to concealment. Their US Topo successor, produced from digital data since 2009, dropped much field-checked detail — notably many trails and some buildings — in favour of an orthophoto layer, which makes modern sheets less useful for backcountry route-finding than the scanned historical ones available through the USGS's own topoView archive. This is a rare case of a national series becoming less informative over time, and it is worth knowing before you rely on a current download. Britain's Ordnance Survey publishes Landranger at 1:50,000 and Explorer at 1:25,000, both with metric contours and both overprinting public rights of way, access land and, on Explorer, field boundaries. The right-of-way overprint has no equivalent in most countries. France's IGN Série Bleue and TOP 25 at 1:25,000 use their own woodland and rock conventions and mark GR long-distance paths distinctly. Switzerland's swisstopo sheets are widely regarded as the finest in the world, using shaded relief and a rock-drawing technique developed by Eduard Imhof in the twentieth century that renders cliffs and scree with an almost photographic legibility no purely symbolic scheme achieves. Military series form a parallel world. NATO Standardization Agreement 3675 and the associated symbol specifications govern Joint Operations Graphics and Topographic Line Maps, imposing consistent symbology across allied nations so that a shared map is unambiguously readable. Military sheets carry the Military Grid Reference System, a grid reference box explaining its use, and are printed so that critical detail survives under red-filtered light at night — which is why some features that would naturally be red are rendered in other colours. Orienteering maps deserve separate mention because they look topographic and are not. Drawn to the International Specification for Orienteering Maps at scales of 1:15,000, 1:10,000 or finer, they invert the usual convention: yellow means open, runnable ground and green means slow going, with darker green meaning slower, so a symbol scheme optimised for foot speed rather than land cover. Contour intervals are typically five metres or less and boulders, pits, root stocks and knolls are mapped individually. Reading one with topographic habits will mislead you badly, and vice versa. The disciplined response to all this is simple and takes thirty seconds: before using any unfamiliar sheet, read its legend end to end, note the contour interval, note the date, note the grid, and note anything that contradicts your expectations. Never assume the symbol you know is the symbol on the page.

sections.heading: Orienting the Sheet and Working the Ground
sections.body: Symbol knowledge only becomes navigation when the map is physically aligned with the world. Orienting — also called setting the map — is the habit that separates people who read maps from people who navigate with them, and it costs nothing but the discipline to keep doing it. The reason it works is that an oriented map removes an entire class of error. When the sheet points the same way as the ground, a feature to your left on the ground appears to your left on the paper, and no mental rotation is required. Mental rotation is exactly the operation that fails under stress, cold and fatigue, and it is the mechanism behind most cases of walking confidently down the wrong valley. Accept that the map will often be upside down relative to its text; reading text at an odd angle beats reversing directions in your head. Once set, work by named techniques rather than by staring. A handrail is a long linear feature parallel to your route that you follow without needing precise bearings — a stream, a wall, a forest edge, a powerline. A catching feature, or backstop, is a large unmistakable feature beyond your target that tells you at once that you have gone too far: a road, a river, a ridgeline. An attack point is a distinct feature close to a hard-to-find target from which you take a short, accurate final bearing — navigate easily to the sheepfold, then take fifty metres on a bearing to the spring. Aiming off means deliberately steering to one side of a target on a linear feature, so that on reaching it you know which way to turn. Cost each leg before you walk it. Naismith's rule, published by William Naismith in 1892, allows one hour per five kilometres plus one hour per six hundred metres of ascent, read straight off the contours by counting index lines; add a third for a heavy pack, a third for darkness and a third for snow. For the final short leg, pace it: count double paces over a measured hundred metres — most adults record sixty to seventy on the flat, considerably more uphill or under load.
steps: Lay the map flat and identify the grid north lines or the true north edge of the sheet.
Place the compass on the map with its long edge along a north-south grid line, needle housing free to turn.
Rotate the whole map, compass on it, until the magnetic needle sits over the orienting arrow, offset by the declination stated in the collar.
Confirm against the ground: pick two visible features and check their relative directions match the sheet.
Fix your position by terrain association, resection from two or three bearings, or a known point such as a junction, summit or bridge.
Choose the next leg to end on a catching feature or an attack point rather than an arbitrary spot.
Note the leg's distance, bearing, ascent and expected time before setting off, and say them aloud to a partner.
Re-orient the map at every stop, every path junction and every change of direction, without exception.

sections.heading: Failure Modes: When the Symbol Lies
sections.body: Maps fail in patterned, predictable ways, and a navigator who knows the patterns treats a contradiction as information rather than panic. The single most important discipline is this: when the ground and the map disagree, the ground is right. The map is a historical document; the hillside is the present tense. The commonest failure is age. Buildings appear and vanish, tracks are bulldozed or abandoned, plantations are felled, quarries expand, rivers migrate across their floodplains, and coastlines erode. A bridge shown on a 1985 survey may have been washed out in a flood decades ago, and the guide who says "there must be a crossing here" because the map says so has inverted the correct relationship between evidence and belief. The second failure is generalisation misread as truth. Displacement in congested corridors means the road, railway and river are not in their true relative positions. A track drawn as a smooth curve had bends removed. A building block at 1:50,000 is a rectangle standing for a village. None of this is error; it is the design working as intended, and problems arise only when a reader demands metre-level truth from a symbol that was never making that claim. The third failure is the symbol whose meaning you assumed. Intermittent streams read as reliable water. White read as open ground on a USGS sheet when it means only "not concealing vegetation". A green right-of-way overprint read as a visible path. A "track" that is a legally gated private estate road. A "spring" that is a stock trough on private land behind a locked gate. Each of these is a vocabulary error, and each is cured by reading the legend rather than trusting habit. The fourth is the invisible feature. A four-metre rock step on a ten-metre contour sheet leaves no mark. A barbed-wire fence, a deep ditch, a cornfield, a bull, a snowbridge, an unstable moraine slope — these are all real obstacles that no topographic symbol set attempts to represent. Contours describe elevation, not difficulty, and smooth contours on a fifty-degree scree slope are perfectly accurate and completely misleading about the experience. The fifth is the reader. Grid reference reversed (northings before eastings). Declination applied in the wrong direction. Contour interval assumed rather than read. Index contours miscounted so you believe you are one loop higher than you are. Map read at ninety degrees because it was never oriented. All of these are procedural errors and all are prevented by procedure: read the collar, orient the sheet, state the leg out loud, and check your position against something independent at least every twenty minutes. The recovery habit that matters most is early admission. Navigational error compounds with distance, so uncertainty at five hundred metres is a minor correction and the same uncertainty at five kilometres may be a rescue. When two consecutive expected features fail to appear, stop. Do not continue in hope. Return to your last certain position if it is safely reachable, or fix your position afresh by resection, altimeter, satellite receiver, or a deliberate walk to a large catching feature such as a river or road.

sections.heading: When the Map Runs Out: Damage, Loss and Improvisation
sections.body: Paper tears, ink runs, sheets blow away, batteries die, and the route leaves the edge of the printed area. The symbol knowledge in your head remains, and it is enough to work with if you have thought about the situation in advance. Protect the sheet before the weather does. Standard topographic paper is not waterproof and loses legibility within minutes of hard rain; a heavy-gauge transparent map case or a laminated sheet solves the problem outright. Fold so that the day's route is on the visible panel, refold under shelter rather than in the wind, and mark the sheet with a chinagraph pencil or fine permanent pen on the case rather than the paper. Carry the route summary — bearings, distances, ascent, escape lines and the grid references of the key points — written on a card in a pocket, because that card weighs nothing and survives the loss of everything else. If the map is destroyed or unavailable, fall back to principles that hold everywhere. Water flows downhill, so following drainage downstream reliably leads toward larger drainage, which leads toward valleys, which is where settlement, roads and rescue concentrate; this is why "follow the water down" is standard survival advice, with the honest caveat that in canyon country and in the tropics it can lead into gorges, waterfalls and impassable vegetation, and in those landscapes ridgelines are the safer descent. High ground gives you signal, sightlines and the chance to identify a landmark. The sun rises broadly east and sets broadly west, with substantial seasonal swing away from the equator, and at local noon its shadow points close to true north in the northern hemisphere and true south in the southern. At night, Polaris sits within about one degree of the celestial north pole and is found by extending the pointer stars of the Plough; the Southern Cross gives an approximate south by extending its long axis about four and a half times. If you have a working satellite receiver but no map, its coordinates are still valuable — recorded and transmitted, they let someone else with a map find you exactly. Write them down rather than trusting the device to survive. The best insurance is redundancy chosen for independent failure modes: a paper sheet and a compass, which need no power, alongside a phone or receiver, which fails when wet or flat. Photographing the map on a phone before departure costs nothing and has resolved a great many minor emergencies. Telling someone your route and expected return time costs nothing and has resolved a great many major ones. Above all, treat symbol literacy as a perishable skill. The vocabulary is small and learnable in an evening, but the fluency that lets you glance at a contour pattern and know, without deliberation, that the far side of the col drops away in a concave slope into a wooded re-entrant — that comes only from repeated, deliberate comparison of map to ground, done in good conditions, long before you need it in bad ones.

guides.title: Reading the Margin of a Topographic Map
guides.summary: How to read everything printed outside the map face of a topographic sheet: scale, datums, grid systems, declination diagrams, edition dates, accuracy statements and legends, and how to use that marginal information to navigate safely.

sections.heading: Why the Margin of a Map Deserves Your Attention
sections.body: A topographic map is really two documents printed on a single sheet. Inside the fine black rectangle that cartographers call the neatline lies the terrain itself: the contours, streams, roads, buildings and names that most people think of as the map. Outside the neatline, in the white border known as the margin or the collar, lies everything a reader must know before a single line of that terrain can be trusted. The margin is the map's contract with its user. It states how much the world has been shrunk, which mathematical model of the Earth the coordinates rest on, how far magnetic north diverges from the map's grid, when the ground was surveyed and when the sheet was last revised, what the symbols and colors mean, and how accurate the makers believe their own work to be. Skipping it means navigating on faith, and the failures that follow are not hypothetical. A hiker who reads coordinates from a modern GPS receiver set to the WGS84 datum and plots them on a 1950s sheet compiled on the North American Datum of 1927 can be off by a hundred meters or more, enough to put a rescue party on the wrong side of a ravine. A traveler who applies a declination value of the wrong sign, because the diagram was never checked, walks two compass errors apart from the intended line: a fifteen degree mistake displaces you roughly 260 meters for every kilometer traveled, since one degree of bearing error costs about 17.5 meters per kilometer. A party trusting a forty-year-old sheet may find that the clear-cut shown as forest, the bridge shown as intact, or the trail shown as maintained no longer exists, and only the edition dates in the margin would have warned them. Professional users treat the margin as the first read, not the last. Military map reading courses begin with marginal information precisely because a grid reference passed over a radio is meaningless unless both parties know the sheet number, series and datum it belongs to. Surveyors, pilots, geologists and search-and-rescue coordinators all follow the same discipline: identify the sheet, confirm the scale and contour interval, confirm the datum, update the declination, and only then look at the terrain. This guide walks through the margin of a typical topographic sheet element by element, using the conventions of the United States Geological Survey quadrangle series and of standard military topographic maps as reference points, because between them these two families set the pattern that most national mapping agencies follow. The details differ from country to country, and from edition to edition within a country, but the categories of information are remarkably stable, and once you can interrogate one nation's margin you can interrogate any of them. The habit takes perhaps three minutes per sheet and it converts a decorative picture of terrain into a measuring instrument whose error bars you actually know.

sections.heading: The Anatomy of a Map Sheet
sections.body: Before reading individual marginal elements it helps to know the geography of the sheet itself, because mapping agencies place information in predictable locations and a practiced eye finds any element in seconds. The map face is bounded by the neatline, the thin line that marks the exact limit of the mapped area; on most quadrangle maps the neatline is itself a graticule, meaning its corners fall on exact values of latitude and longitude. Immediately outside the neatline runs the border, often a heavier line or a banded frame carrying coordinate ticks and labels. Everything beyond that is the collar. Along the top of a United States Geological Survey sheet you will find the agency name at upper left, the sheet name at upper right, and often the state and series designation beside it. The bottom margin is the dense zone: at lower left sit the credit legend and production notes, which record who compiled the map, from what source material, in what year, on what datum and projection; at bottom center sit the scale statement, the bar scales, the contour interval note and the accuracy statement; at lower right the sheet name repeats together with the location diagram and road classification legend. The declination diagram usually sits in the bottom margin as well, toward the left or center. Military sheets in the standard NATO pattern arrange things differently but no less predictably: the sheet name at top center, the series and sheet number in the corners, and a bottom margin that carries, reading across, the legend box, the scale bars, the projection and grid notes, the grid reference box with a worked example of how to report a coordinate, the declination diagram, boundary and adjoining-sheet diagrams, and a users' note inviting corrections. Two practical consequences follow from this layout. First, the sheet name appears in at least two corners on nearly every national series, usually upper right and lower right, so a folded map can be identified without opening it fully; experienced navigators fold maps so a named corner faces outward. Second, the information density of the bottom margin is why you should never trim the collar off a map to save weight or to mount it, at least not before copying the critical values onto the face or into a notebook. A trimmed sheet has lost its datum, its declination, its contour interval and its edition date, and each of those losses is a navigation error waiting for its moment. When agencies print maps for water resistance or issue digital versions such as the US Topo series in PDF form, the collar survives as a layer or panel, and the same reading order applies. Learn the layout of the national series you use most, then confirm it on every unfamiliar sheet, because provincial series, private publishers and older editions do move elements around, and the only safe assumption is that everything important is somewhere in the margin waiting to be found.

sections.heading: Sheet Name, Series and Edition
sections.body: The identity block of a map answers three questions: where is this, which map family does it belong to, and how current is it. The sheet name on a civilian quadrangle is usually taken from a prominent settlement or natural feature on the sheet, and it is unique only within its series and state or province, which is why the name is always paired with a series designation. The United States Geological Survey's flagship series is the 7.5-minute quadrangle: each sheet spans 7.5 minutes of latitude by 7.5 minutes of longitude, drawn at a scale of 1:24,000, and roughly 57,000 such sheets cover the contiguous United States. Older 15-minute maps at 1:62,500, metric 1:25,000 and 1:100,000 sheets, and the 1:250,000 series exist alongside them, and the series statement in the margin is what tells you which family you hold. Military maps carry a formal series number such as V745, a sheet number derived from a global reference scheme, and an edition number such as Edition 3-DMA, where the suffix identifies the producing agency. The edition line matters more than any other part of the identity block, because it encodes the map's age in a way that a casual glance at the print date does not. A margin note reading Compiled 1954, photorevised 1976 tells you that the base mapping, including contours, reflects surveys and aerial photography from the early 1950s, and that changes detected on 1976 photography were added, traditionally overprinted in purple, without full field verification. Purple features on such a sheet mean this appeared on photographs but no one walked the ground to confirm it. A separate imprint date records only when the paper went through the press and says nothing about the currency of the content, a distinction that has misled generations of buyers who assumed a recently printed map was a recently surveyed one. Modern digital products complicate the picture in a different way: a US Topo sheet regenerated on a three-year cycle carries current imagery and roads drawn from national databases, yet its contours may still descend from the original mid-century compilation, so even a map dated last year can carry sixty-year-old elevation art. When you pick up any sheet, therefore, extract three dates if they exist: the survey or compilation date, which governs the terrain depiction; the revision or photorevision date, which governs cultural features like roads and buildings; and the print or edition date, which governs only the paper. Judge each class of feature by its own date. Contours age slowly, since hillsides rarely move; glaciers, rivers, coastlines and human construction age quickly, and in fast-developing or fire-prone country a ten-year-old cultural layer is a rumor rather than a record. Writing the governing dates on the face of the map in pencil when you first read the margin is a habit that pays for itself the first time you plan a route after dark.

sections.heading: Scale, the Representative Fraction and the Bar Scales
sections.body: The scale statement is the single most-read element of any margin, and it is expressed in two complementary forms. The representative fraction, written 1:24,000 or 1:50,000, states that one unit of any kind on the map equals that many of the same units on the ground: one centimeter equals 240 meters at 1:24,000, one inch equals 2,000 feet, and the fraction is unitless, which is what makes it universal. A useful mental anchor is that at 1:25,000 four centimeters represent one kilometer, at 1:50,000 two centimeters do, and at 1:100,000 one centimeter does. Larger scale means a larger fraction and a smaller area shown in more detail, so 1:24,000 is a larger scale than 1:250,000, a phrasing that trips up newcomers constantly. Beneath the fraction sit the graphic bar scales, typically three of them on an American sheet, graduated in miles, feet and kilometers. Bar scales have two properties the fraction lacks. First, they include an extension scale: the divisions to the left of zero are subdivided finely, so you measure a distance by laying a paper edge or string along your route, placing one tick mark on a whole division to the right of zero, and reading the remainder in the fine divisions to the left. Second, and more subtly, the bar scale is the only scale statement that remains honest when the sheet itself changes size. Paper is a humidity sensor; a map can shrink or swell by one or two percent between a dry winter room and a wet tent, and any photocopy or print-at-home PDF may be enlarged or reduced without warning. The printed fraction becomes a lie under those conditions, but the bar scale, having shrunk or stretched with the paper, still measures the map correctly. For this reason careful navigators measure with the bar scale or with a romer matched to the sheet, and treat ruler-plus-fraction arithmetic as a fair-weather method. Distance measured on any map is horizontal distance, the length of your route projected onto a level surface, and the margin's scale says nothing about the extra length you will walk climbing and descending; on a slope of 30 degrees the ground distance exceeds the map distance by about 15 percent, and a route with a thousand meters of ascent and descent adds real kilometers that no scale bar shows. Slope also interacts with scale when you estimate gradient: at 1:24,000 with a 40-foot contour interval, contours spaced one millimeter apart represent a slope of roughly 27 degrees, and learning a few such anchors for your usual map family lets you read steepness at a glance. Finally, check that the scale printed matches the scale you assumed. Series at 1:25,000 and 1:24,000 look almost identical, but a four percent error compounds over a long route, and sheets from different series do not join at their edges. The margin states the truth; the reader's job is merely to believe it rather than habit.

sections.heading: The Contour Interval and the Vertical Datum
sections.body: Directly beneath the bar scales a short line of text does an outsized share of the map's work: Contour interval 40 feet, or 10 meters, or whatever value the terrain and scale demanded. The contour interval is the vertical distance between adjacent contour lines, and every judgment you make about steepness, climb and visibility depends on knowing it. American 7.5-minute sheets commonly use 40 feet in mountainous country, 20 feet in rolling country and 10 or even 5 feet in flat river plains; metric sheets typically use 20 meters at 1:50,000 and 10 meters at 1:25,000. The interval is chosen per sheet, not per series, so two adjoining maps can differ, and a party crossing from one sheet to the next has misjudged a climb by a factor of two for exactly this reason. The margin may also announce supplementary contours, usually dashed lines at half the standard interval, added where the ground is so flat that full-interval contours would say nothing; if you ignore the note you will read a dashed supplementary as a full step of elevation and double the relief in your head. In depressions, small closed contours carry hachures, short ticks pointing downslope, and the legend or margin confirms the convention. The companion statement to the interval is the vertical datum, the zero surface from which all elevations on the sheet are measured. Older American maps reference the National Geodetic Vertical Datum of 1929, abbreviated NGVD 29 and once called mean sea level datum; newer mapping references the North American Vertical Datum of 1988, NAVD 88. The difference between the two surfaces varies geographically from roughly minus 40 centimeters to plus 150 centimeters across the contiguous United States, which is irrelevant to a hiker judging a climb but decisive to anyone using the map for flood elevations, benchmark work or engineering, and the margin is the only place the map declares which surface it means. Coastal sheets add further datums: depth curves and soundings on the water portion of a topographic-bathymetric sheet are measured not from the land datum but from a tidal datum such as mean lower low water, and the marginal note is the only warning that land elevations and water depths on the same sheet share no common zero. Benchmark symbols on the face, marked BM with an elevation, record precisely surveyed points tied to the stated datum, and spot elevations without the BM tag are less rigorous photogrammetric values. When you read the margin, say the interval out loud and write it on the face of the map near your route. It is the one number you will use every hour of a mountain day, it cannot be recovered from the contours themselves without a known elevation difference, and confusing feet with meters, easy to do when you alternate between American and metric sheets, inflates or deflates every climb by a factor of three.

sections.heading: Horizontal Datums and Why GPS Cares
sections.body: A horizontal datum is the reference frame that gives meaning to latitude, longitude and grid coordinates: a mathematical model of the Earth's shape together with a rule for attaching it to the physical planet. The margin of every serious topographic map names its datum, and no coordinate on the sheet means anything without it. Older North American mapping rests on the North American Datum of 1927, NAD 27, built on the Clarke 1866 ellipsoid and anchored at a survey station called Meades Ranch in Kansas; the continent's coordinates were adjusted outward from that single point by triangulation. Satellite geodesy replaced this regional construction with Earth-centered datums: the North American Datum of 1983, NAD 83, and the World Geodetic System 1984, WGS 84, which is the native reference of the Global Positioning System. For most practical navigation NAD 83 and WGS 84 can be treated as identical, their difference being a meter or two, but NAD 27 differs from both substantially: converting a coordinate from NAD 27 to NAD 83 shifts it by an amount that varies with location, typically tens of meters and up to well over one hundred meters in parts of the western United States, Alaska and Hawaii. The consequences are concrete. If your GPS receiver is set to WGS 84 and you plot its readout on an NAD 27 sheet, the plotted point can sit the length of a football field from where you are standing, an error that has sent searchers to the wrong drainage more than once. The defenses are equally concrete. First, read the datum note in the credit legend of every sheet you use; on USGS quadrangles it appears in the lower left, often with a small diagram showing the shift to NAD 83 for that sheet expressed in meters or in fractions of the grid. Second, set your receiver or mapping application to the map's datum when you intend to plot on paper, or convert coordinates deliberately; every serious receiver since the 1990s can display positions in dozens of datums precisely because paper maps outlive datum transitions. Third, when exchanging coordinates with another party, state the datum as part of the coordinate, exactly as you state units with a measurement; a grid reference without a datum is a number without a unit. The rest of the world tells the same story with different names: Great Britain's maps rest on OSGB36, continental Europe used ED50 before ETRS89, Japan used Tokyo Datum before JGD2000, and in each case the shift to WGS 84 amounts to tens or hundreds of meters. Datum confusion is invisible on the map face, is not detectable by common sense, and is entirely preventable by reading one line of small print. Of everything in the margin, this line is the one that GPS-era navigators can least afford to skip.

sections.heading: Projection Notes and Grid Systems
sections.body: Because the Earth is round and paper is flat, every map embodies a projection, a mathematical rule for flattening a curved surface, and the margin names it. Most large-scale topographic mapping uses a conformal projection, one that preserves angles and local shapes at the cost of slightly distorting scale, because a navigator's compass work depends on angles being true. American quadrangles historically used a polyconic projection and later a transverse Mercator; military mapping worldwide standardized on the Universal Transverse Mercator system, UTM, which divides the world into sixty north-south zones, each six degrees of longitude wide, numbered eastward from the 180th meridian. Within each zone, positions are stated in meters: an easting measured from a value of 500,000 meters assigned to the zone's central meridian, so that no easting is ever negative, and a northing measured from the equator, with the southern hemisphere given a false northing of 10,000,000 meters. The central meridian is drawn at a scale factor of 0.9996, meaning distances along it are deliberately shown four parts in ten thousand too small so that distortion at the zone edges stays within one part in a thousand, a detail the margin sometimes states and which matters only to surveyors. What matters to navigators is the grid: the fine lines ruled across the face at one-kilometer intervals on 1:24,000 through 1:100,000 sheets, labeled along the margins with their easting and northing values, principal digits printed large. The margin tells you the grid's zone, its datum, and, on military sheets, the grid reference box walks you through reporting a position to any precision: a six-figure reference such as 123456 names a point to the nearest hundred meters, eight figures to ten meters, read right then up, eastings before northings. The Military Grid Reference System, MGRS, layers letter codes for zone and 100,000-meter square onto the same numbers so that a full reference like 18TWL8040 is unambiguous worldwide. Some margins also show ticks for other grids: state plane coordinates on American sheets, national grids such as Britain's, or the older land-survey framework of township and range lines printed in red. A margin can therefore carry three or four coordinate systems simultaneously, and part of reading it is deciding which one you and your companions will speak. Choose one, confirm everyone's receivers display it, and confirm the zone, because identical-looking coordinates recur in every zone on Earth. Note also the fine print about grid declination: grid north and true north coincide only along each zone's central meridian, diverging by up to about three degrees at the edges, which is why the declination diagram nearby shows three norths rather than two. The projection itself you may never need to think about again; the grid it generates you will use every time you state where you are.

sections.heading: The Declination Diagram: Three Norths
sections.body: Near the bottom margin of nearly every topographic sheet stands a small diagram of two or three diverging rays, and misreading it is among the most common causes of navigation error. The rays represent the three norths a map user must keep distinct. True north, usually drawn with a star for Polaris, is the direction along your meridian to the geographic North Pole; the map's neatline sides point true north on a graticule- bounded quadrangle. Grid north, labeled GN, is the direction of the vertical grid lines, which align with true north only at the projection zone's central meridian and elsewhere diverge by a stated angle, rarely more than about three degrees. Magnetic north, drawn with a half arrowhead and labeled MN, is where a balanced compass needle actually points, toward the wandering north magnetic pole, and its divergence from true north is the magnetic declination, while its divergence from grid north is the grid-magnetic angle, or G-M angle, the number a grid-based navigator actually uses. The margin states these angles in degrees, and on military sheets also in mils, the artillery unit of which there are 6,400 to a circle, so one mil is about 0.056 degrees; small angles are often given entirely in mils. Two warnings are printed or implied beside every such diagram and both are routinely ignored. First, the diagram is not drawn to scale: a declination of one and a half degrees would be invisible if drawn truly, so the rays are exaggerated for legibility, and measuring the diagram with a protractor is an error. Use the printed numbers only. Second, the values are true only for the stated date and the sheet's center; declination varies across a single sheet by a fraction of a degree and across a continent by tens of degrees, from roughly 15 degrees east on the American west coast to 15 degrees west in the northeast, with the agonic line of zero declination currently crossing the Mississippi valley. The arithmetic of applying declination is where signs go wrong, and the safest formulation is worth memorizing in one direction: to convert a magnetic bearing taken with a compass into a true bearing, add easterly declination and subtract westerly. To go from map to compass, reverse the operation. Many compasses allow you to set the declination once on an adjustable ring, after which the needle reads true or grid bearings directly, and in areas of large declination this is worth doing before travel, with the setting written on the map face. Whatever method you choose, rehearse it with a known case before you need it in fog: from a marked summit, take a bearing to a visible neighbor, work the conversion, and confirm the map agrees. The diagram gives you the numbers; only practice gives you the signs.

sections.heading: Keeping Declination Current
sections.body: Magnetic declination is the one value in the margin that expires. The Earth's field is generated by convection in the liquid outer core, and its secular variation drifts the magnetic poles continuously; the north magnetic pole has moved from arctic Canada toward Siberia at rates that accelerated from about 15 kilometers per year in the early twentieth century to roughly 50 to 55 kilometers per year around 2015, slowing somewhat since. Mapping agencies therefore print the declination with a date and, on many series, an annual change note such as mean annual change 6 minutes westward. Reading these two lines and doing thirty seconds of arithmetic is part of reading the margin. Consider a sheet printed in 1985 stating a declination of 12 degrees east with an annual change of 6 minutes westerly. By 2026, forty-one years have passed; forty-one times six minutes is 246 minutes, about 4.1 degrees, applied westward, giving a present declination of roughly 7.9 degrees east. On a 2 kilometer leg in poor visibility, using the stale 12-degree value instead would place you about 140 meters off your intended point, since each degree of bearing error displaces you about 17.5 meters per kilometer traveled. Two honest cautions accompany the arithmetic. First, the printed annual change is itself a snapshot; secular variation is not linear, and extrapolating more than a decade or two beyond the map date multiplies error, so for maps older than about fifteen years the annual-change method should be treated as an estimate rather than a correction. Second, the authoritative answer at any moment comes from a geomagnetic reference model, the World Magnetic Model produced jointly by the American and British geological agencies and revised every five years, or the International Geomagnetic Reference Field; any current declination calculator, many GPS receivers and most smartphone compass applications embed one of these models and will give the declination for your exact coordinates and date to a fraction of a degree. The careful workflow is therefore: read the map's stated declination and date, update it either by the annual-change note or, better, from a current model before travel, write the current value in pencil beside the diagram, and set it on your compass if the instrument allows. One more marginal note deserves respect: some sheets in volcanic, iron-rich or mineralized country carry a warning that local magnetic disturbance makes compass readings unreliable in parts of the sheet, and such anomalies can reach tens of degrees within meters of magnetite-bearing rock. No model corrects for those; the note exists so that when your needle misbehaves near a basalt outcrop you distrust the needle rather than the map. Declination is not a difficulty, merely a discipline: dated value in, current value out, written down, set once, rechecked whenever the map or the decade changes.

sections.heading: Adjoining Sheets, Location Diagrams and Boundaries
sections.body: No journey of consequence stays on one sheet, and the margin provides the tools for stepping off the edge. The adjoining sheet diagram, printed on most series as a small three-by-three grid with the current sheet in the center, names the eight neighboring sheets so you can order or pull the next map before you need it. On older American quadrangles the same information was given more economically: the name of the adjacent quadrangle printed in parentheses at the center of each edge and at each corner, so that the sheet you would enter by walking off the east edge is named on the east margin. Military series use an index to adjoining sheets keyed by sheet number, and national atlas-style indexes map every sheet number in the series onto a national outline, which is how you plan coverage for an expedition in the first place. A separate location diagram, usually a small state or country outline with a black rectangle, shows where the sheet sits in the larger world, which sounds trivial until you are sorting forty unfamiliar quadrangles on a floor. Some series add a boundaries diagram, an index to the civil divisions on the sheet, counties, districts, municipalities, reserves, so that a jurisdiction can be identified without cluttering the face; on military maps this matters for coordination with civil authorities, and for a civilian it answers the practical question of whose land regulations, hunting seasons or emergency services apply where you are standing. Reading these diagrams carefully repays you in three specific situations. First, route planning: if your route crosses a sheet corner, you may need four maps for a single day, a fact only the adjoining diagram makes obvious, and corner crossings are notorious for being discovered at home the night before. Second, edge matching: sheets of the same series and edition join cleanly, but where editions differ the roads may have been realigned, the datum may differ on very old pairs, and contour intervals can change at the join, so the margin of each sheet must be read separately rather than assuming the pair agrees. Third, communication: when reporting a position near a sheet boundary by grid reference, the sheet number from the margin removes the ambiguity of which map's grid you mean, and search-and-rescue protocols commonly require sheet number alongside the grid. It is worth a caution that publishers of recreational maps sometimes recenter their sheets on popular areas precisely so that a famous mountain does not fall on a corner; the adjoining diagram tells you whether you hold such a convenience product or a rigid national grid of quadrangles. Either way, the margin's little grid of names is the map's confession that the world continues beyond the neatline, and the competent navigator answers it by carrying the neighbors.

sections.heading: The Legend: Symbols, Colors and Their Dialects
sections.body: The legend translates the map's graphic language, and although experienced users internalize most of it, the margin remains the arbiter whenever a symbol is ambiguous, because symbol dialects differ between countries, series and decades. The color conventions of topographic mapping are broadly stable: brown for contours and other relief such as sand and tailings; blue for water in all its forms, including the intermittent streams whose dash-and-dot pattern distinguishes them from perennial ones; green for vegetation dense enough to matter, historically defined on American sheets as cover capable of concealing troops; black for cultural features built by people, buildings, tracks, boundaries and names; red for principal roads, built-up area tints and the land-survey grid; and purple for features added by photorevision without field check. White on the face is not blank paper in meaning: it denotes open ground, grassland, tundra, rock or snowfield depending on context, and distinguishing them requires contours and judgment rather than the legend alone. Within each color the legend earns its keep on the marginal cases. Road classifications, drawn as paired lines, single lines and dashes, encode passability claims: the difference between an improved light-duty road and an unimproved track is the difference between driving and walking, and the classification key in the margin is the only place the claim is defined. Trail symbols on older sheets do not distinguish maintained from abandoned routes. Marsh symbols, tufted blue clusters, mark ground that may be impassable in spring and firm in late summer. Cliff and escarpment symbols, hachured brown lines, appear only where the drop is significant at map scale, so their absence never proves the absence of a cliff, a point the accuracy standards section of the margin quietly reinforces. Mine symbols, crossed pick and hammer, and the associated shaft and adit marks warn of hazards that attract exactly the curiosity they should repel. American 7.5-minute sheets print only an abbreviated road legend in the margin and publish the full symbol dictionary as a separate booklet, a fact the margin itself states, whereas military sheets and most European national series print a complete legend box on every sheet; if you navigate on a series with an abbreviated legend, the full key belongs in your map case. Two habits make the legend genuinely useful rather than decorative. When planning, run your eyes down the legend once per unfamiliar series, specifically noting how it draws the features that decide routes: bridges, fords, gates, springs, huts and power lines. And when a symbol on the face puzzles you, resist inference from appearance; symbols are conventions, not pictures, and the tuft that looks like grass may be defined as submerged marsh. The legend is short, and reading it completely is the cheapest competence in navigation.

sections.heading: Accuracy Statements, Reliability and Source Notes
sections.body: The most modest sentence in the margin is also the most philosophically important: the accuracy statement, which tells you how wrong the map is permitted to be. American quadrangles carry the note that the map complies with National Map Accuracy Standards, a specification issued in 1941 and revised in 1947 that remains the reference for the paper series. Its horizontal test requires that at publication scales smaller than 1:20,000, at least 90 percent of well-defined points, road intersections, building corners, bench marks, fall within one-fiftieth of an inch of their true position on the sheet; at 1:24,000 that tolerance is 40 feet, about 12 meters, on the ground. The vertical test requires that 90 percent of elevations interpolated from the contours be correct within half the contour interval, so on a 40-foot-interval sheet any contour-derived elevation carries a tacit error bar of 20 feet, and one point in ten may be worse. Reading those numbers recalibrates expectations wholesomely: a GPS receiver reporting your position to three meters is now more precise than the map under it, and disagreement between receiver and map within a dozen meters is not evidence that either is broken. The standards also explain mapping conventions that otherwise look like errors: features too small to plot accurately are exaggerated or displaced for legibility, roads and the streams beside them are separated on the sheet though they touch on the ground, and small buildings are shown by standardized symbols larger than their true footprints. Military and many international sheets go further and print a reliability diagram, a small index dividing the sheet into areas by the quality and date of source material, compiled from 1:40,000 photography 1972, derived from older mapping, field completed or not, so that one corner of the map may be certified trustworthy and another explicitly second-hand. The credit note in the lower left corner of an American sheet serves the same purpose in prose: it names the compilation method, aerial photographs and photogrammetric methods, the dates of photography and field check, the datum, the projection and the agencies responsible. Older sheets surveyed by plane table before aerial methods carry their own note and their own error character, generous in well-traveled valleys and imaginative on remote ridges. The practical reading is always the same three questions: how was this made, when, and to what tested tolerance. Where the margin answers them well, trust the map to its stated limits. Where a sheet carries no accuracy statement at all, common with tourist maps and some private publishers, assume the cartography is illustrative, verify critical features against a governmental series, and never bet a night descent on an unattested contour.

sections.heading: Reading Coordinates from the Border
sections.body: The border between neatline and collar is an instrument in its own right: it carries the tick marks and labels from which every coordinate on the sheet is derived. On a standard quadrangle the four corners are labeled with their full latitude and longitude, for example 44 degrees 15 minutes north, 71 degrees 22 minutes 30 seconds west, and because a 7.5-minute sheet spans exactly 7.5 minutes each way, the opposite corners differ by that amount. Along each edge, small ticks subdivide the span at 2.5-minute intervals, labeled with abbreviated values, so the graticule can be reconstructed by connecting opposite ticks with a straightedge; most modern sheets print small crosses on the face where these graticule lines intersect, and drawing the connecting lines in pencil converts the sheet into a latitude-longitude plotting surface. To read a geographic coordinate, measure your point's fraction of the distance between two adjacent ticks and interpolate: a point 40 percent of the way from the 12-minute-30-second tick toward the 15-minute tick lies at 13 minutes 30 seconds. The UTM grid is labeled differently and used more easily. Grid line values appear along all four edges in a distinctive style: the principal digits, the two large numerals that change from line to line, printed bold, with the full value, such as 4,868,000 meters north, spelled out once near a corner. To state a position, read right then up. Find the grid line left of your point and take its principal digits, estimate tenths of the square eastward to your point, then find the grid line below and do the same northward: easting 80 and four tenths, northing 68 and seven tenths yields the six-figure reference 804687, locating you within a hundred-meter square. A transparent romer or the grid scales printed in some margins turn the estimation of tenths into a direct reading, and an eight-figure reference read the same way narrows the square to ten meters. Precision claims deserve honesty: a six-figure reference read by eye is realistic from a folded map on a knee in wind; ten-meter claims require a romer, a flat surface and care. Two traps recur. On maps where the grid belongs to a different zone along the sheet edge, a secondary set of ticks appears in the margin, and mixing the two produces coordinates in the wrong zone; the margin labels them, so read the labels. And on sheets where the grid is drawn from one datum and the graticule from another, older transitional printings did exactly this, the fine print beside the corner values is the only warning. The border rewards slow first acquaintance: find the corner values, trace one graticule line, read one grid value aloud, and thereafter the sheet will answer position questions as fast as you can lay a straightedge on it.

sections.heading: A Margin Check Before Every Journey
sections.body: Marginal information turns into safety only when reading it becomes a ritual, and the ritual is short enough to survive real trips. The full check of an unfamiliar sheet takes about three minutes; the refresher on a known sheet takes thirty seconds, and both are best done at the planning table rather than in wind and failing light. The procedure below compresses everything the margin offers into a fixed order, chosen so that each item feeds the next: identity before scale, scale before vertical, vertical before datum, datum before grid, grid before declination, and everything before the terrain is allowed to seduce you. The outputs are physical: values written in pencil on the face of the map near your route, a declination set on the compass if it adjusts, and the neighboring sheets located or acquired. Writing on the map matters because the margin may be folded away, soaked, or trimmed on the copy you actually carry, and because a value transcribed in comfort is a value you will not have to derive in trouble. Crews and families should perform the check aloud together so that every navigator in the party carries the same numbers; disagreement discovered at the trailhead is a gift, the same disagreement discovered at a foggy junction is an incident. Repeat the full check whenever any element changes: a new sheet, a new edition of an old sheet, a borrowed map, a photocopied section, a different country's series, or simply the passage of years since the declination was last updated. Treat a missing item as information in itself; a sheet that states no datum, no accuracy note and no edition date has told you exactly how far to trust it. The checklist assumes a paper sheet, but every item applies to digital maps as well, where the collar hides behind an information button and is even easier to ignore: a phone application displaying seamless tiles is still built on source mapping with a compilation date, a datum and an accuracy pedigree, and the failure modes are identical even when the margin is invisible. However you carry your map, the discipline is the same: interrogate the margin first, write down what it says, and only then plan the route. Navigators who practice this report the same experience: the check surfaces one surprise per unfamiliar sheet on average, an unexpected contour interval, a datum older than the navigator, a declination that has drifted three degrees, and each surprise caught at the table is an error that never happens on the hill.
steps: 1. Identify the sheet: read the name, series, sheet number and state or region from the corners, and note them in your route plan.
2. Extract the dates: compilation or survey date, revision or photorevision date, and print date; write the governing dates on the map face.
3. Confirm the scale: read the representative fraction, then check the bar scales against a ruler if the sheet is a copy or printout.
4. Read the contour interval and its units, note any supplementary contour statement, and write the interval beside your route.
5. Read the vertical datum note if elevations matter to your task, especially near coasts or for flood and engineering work.
6. Read the horizontal datum, set your GPS receiver or app to match or plan a deliberate conversion, and record the datum with every coordinate you share.
7. Identify the grid: UTM zone or national grid, confirm which edge ticks belong to it, and agree with your party on one coordinate language.
8. Read the declination diagram: note the stated values, their date and the annual change, compute or look up the current declination, write it beside the diagram, and set an adjustable compass.
9. Check the adjoining sheet diagram against your route and acquire any neighboring sheets it crosses.
10. Scan the legend for the symbols that decide your route, roads, trails, bridges, water, cliffs, and read the accuracy or reliability statement to calibrate trust.

sections.heading: When the Margin Fails You
sections.body: Sooner or later you will navigate on a map whose margin is missing, stale or wrong, and the final competence is knowing how to proceed with degraded metadata. The commonest case is the trimmed or photocopied sheet: a section copied for weight or shared by a companion, carrying terrain but no collar. Treat it as a picture until you restore its numbers. Scale can be recovered from the grid if any grid lines survive, since their spacing is one kilometer on most national series, or from a feature of known length; contour interval can be recovered by finding a labeled index contour, the heavier line usually numbered every fourth or fifth interval, and dividing the elevation difference between two labels by the lines between them. Datum and declination cannot be recovered from the face at all, which is the argument for writing them there before copying. The second case is the obsolete sheet. Terrain endures but its dressing changes: reservoirs drown valleys, glaciers retreat hundreds of meters per decade in many ranges, braided rivers move, logging roads appear and vanish, and coastal barrier islands migrate. Navigate old sheets by their durable skeleton, ridgelines, summits, drainage patterns, and distrust their perishables, structures, vegetation boundaries, trail alignments, water edges. Cross-check anything critical against a second source: a newer map, current satellite imagery cached before departure, or local knowledge, and when two sources disagree, plan routes that fail safely, lines that remain navigable whichever source is right. The third case is the wrong margin: misprints are rare in national series but real, declination diagrams have been printed with reversed sign in commercial reproductions, and grid labels on hastily produced emergency mapping have carried transposed digits. The defense is consistency checking, which costs a minute: does the stated declination match a model value for the region, does a measured grid square equal the bar-scale kilometer, does a labeled summit elevation agree with the contour count. Any single disagreement means stop and resolve; instruments and margins fail independently, so agreement between two independent checks is strong evidence. The last case is no map at all but a mapping application, where the margin has been abstracted into metadata screens nobody opens. The same interrogation applies: find the imagery and mapping dates in the layer information, find the datum your coordinates display in the settings, and export or write down what you learn while you have signal. Margins fail; the habit of asking marginal questions, what scale, what datum, what date, what accuracy, does not depend on the answers being printed, and carrying those four questions in your head is the portable version of everything this guide contains.

guides.title: How Topographic Map Series Are Organised
guides.summary: Why national mapping comes in numbered sheets, and how scale, datum, projection, grid, sheet numbering, contour interval and marginal information fit together. Covers the major national series, magnetic declination, revision cycles and how to choose and prepare sheets for a journey.

sections.heading: Why Countries Map Themselves in Numbered Sheets
sections.body: A topographic map shows the shape of the land along with everything fixed upon it: relief, watercourses, vegetation, roads, buildings, boundaries and place names. The moment you try to make one for a whole country at a useful level of detail, an unavoidable arithmetic problem appears. Great Britain at a scale of one to fifty thousand, printed as a single sheet, would be roughly twenty metres tall. The United States at the scale its classic quadrangles used would be a sheet the size of a football pitch several times over. No press can print that, no person can carry it, and no surveyor could revise it without reprinting the whole thing. The only workable answer is to cut the country into pieces, and once you start cutting, you have created a series. Everything that follows in this subject is a consequence of that decision. Pieces need boundaries, so somebody must decide whether the cuts follow lines of latitude and longitude or the straight lines of a rectangular grid. Pieces need names, so somebody must design a numbering scheme that lets a user holding one sheet work out which sheet lies to the north. Pieces must join, so adjacent sheets must use the same mathematical model of the Earth, the same projection, the same symbols and, ideally, the same survey date, or features will fail to line up across the join. Pieces get revised at different times, so each must carry its own edition information. And because a series may run to tens of thousands of sheets, all of this must be systematic rather than improvised. The people who built the first national series understood that they were building infrastructure rather than publishing books. Britain's Ordnance Survey was founded in 1791 by the Board of Ordnance, prompted by the military need for accurate mapping of the Scottish Highlands after the Jacobite rising and by fear of French invasion on the south coast. The Cassini family's survey of France, carried out between roughly 1750 and 1815, was the first complete topographic survey of an entire country. The United States Geological Survey, founded in 1879, began systematic topographic mapping in 1884. In every case the driver was the same: a state that intends to move armies, levy taxes, build railways or manage land needs to know the shape of its territory to a consistent standard everywhere, not just where somebody happened to be interested. The result is that a map series is a designed system with internal logic, and learning that logic pays off immediately. A reader who understands how sheets are bounded and numbered can find the right map without a catalogue, can predict what will be missing near an edge, can tell at a glance whether a sheet is compatible with a satellite receiver, and can judge how much of what is printed can still be trusted.

sections.heading: Scale and What the Representative Fraction Actually Means
sections.body: Scale is expressed as a representative fraction, a ratio without units. A scale of one to fifty thousand means that any distance measured on the map corresponds to fifty thousand of the same units on the ground. Because the units cancel, the statement works in any measurement system: one centimetre on the map is fifty thousand centimetres, which is five hundred metres, on the ground, and one inch is fifty thousand inches. The practical conversions worth memorising are that at one to fifty thousand, two centimetres make a kilometre; at one to twenty five thousand, four centimetres make a kilometre; and at the older British one inch series of one to sixty three thousand three hundred and sixty, one inch makes exactly one mile, which is where that odd looking number comes from. The terminology reverses most people's intuition and causes constant confusion. A one to twenty five thousand map is called a larger scale than a one to two hundred and fifty thousand map, even though it covers a much smaller area. The reason is that the representative fraction is genuinely a fraction: one twenty five thousandth is a larger number than one two hundred and fifty thousandth. Large scale means large fraction, which means more detail over less ground. A useful mental substitution is to think of large scale as zoomed in and small scale as zoomed out. Series cluster into recognisable scale bands because each band answers a different question. Between one to ten thousand and one to twenty five thousand you get individual buildings, field boundaries, footpaths and fine contour detail, which is what walkers, foresters and land managers need. One to fifty thousand is the classic general purpose topographic scale and the standard for military mapping worldwide, detailed enough to navigate on foot while covering a day's travel on one sheet. One to one hundred thousand through one to two hundred and fifty thousand serves road travel and regional planning. From one to five hundred thousand to one to one million you are into aviation charts and country level overviews, where individual buildings have vanished entirely. The reason detail must drop as scale shrinks is not simply space but legibility. A road drawn to true width at one to fifty thousand would be a fifth of a millimetre across and invisible, so it is drawn exaggerated and displaced, and neighbouring features are shifted to make room. This process, called cartographic generalisation, means a small scale map is not a photographic reduction of a large scale one. Features are selected, simplified, exaggerated and moved by deliberate decision. Consequently a position scaled off a one to two hundred and fifty thousand sheet may be a couple of hundred metres from the truth even when the map is perfectly correct, which matters enormously if you are trying to walk to it.

sections.heading: The Shape of the Earth: Ellipsoids, Datums and Why They Differ
sections.body: Before anything can be mapped, the mappers must agree on what shape they are mapping. The Earth is not a sphere. Its rotation makes it bulge at the equator and flatten at the poles, so the best simple model is an oblate ellipsoid. In the modern global model known as WGS 84, the equatorial radius is 6,378.137 kilometres and the polar radius is 6,356.752 kilometres, a difference of about twenty one kilometres, described by a flattening of about one part in 298.26. That may sound small, but on a map at one to twenty five thousand it is the difference between a position being right and being a kilometre wrong. An ellipsoid alone is not enough. You also have to fix where it sits relative to the actual planet, and that combination of a chosen ellipsoid plus its positioning and orientation is called a geodetic datum. Historically each country chose an ellipsoid that fitted its own territory well and anchored it at a convenient survey station, which produced excellent local accuracy and total global incompatibility. Britain's OSGB36 uses the Airy ellipsoid of 1830. North America used the Clarke ellipsoid of 1866 in the datum called NAD 27. Japan used the Tokyo Datum, based on the Bessel ellipsoid of 1841. Each was a good regional fit and none agrees with the others. The size of the disagreement is the practical point, because satellite receivers report positions in WGS 84 by default and a great many printed maps are not on WGS 84. Coordinates on NAD 27 differ from modern values by anything from about twenty metres to well over two hundred metres depending on where you are in North America. British OSGB36 coordinates differ from WGS 84 by roughly a hundred metres in parts of the country. The old Tokyo Datum was out by roughly four hundred metres in Japan, which is enough to place you on the wrong side of a ridge. Plotting a satellite position onto a map without checking the datum is one of the few genuinely dangerous mistakes in navigation, and it produces errors that are large, consistent and entirely invisible unless you look for them. Datums also move because continents move. Australia sits on a plate travelling northeast at about seven centimetres a year, so its national datum was redefined from GDA 94 to GDA 2020, a deliberate shift of about 1.8 metres to reabsorb three decades of drift. Heights add a further complication: an ellipsoid is a smooth mathematical surface, while sea level follows the geoid, the lumpy equipotential surface of the Earth's gravity field, which departs from the ellipsoid by up to about a hundred metres in places. Satellite receivers measure height above the ellipsoid, whereas maps quote height above a sea level datum, and the two can differ by tens of metres.

sections.heading: Projections and Why Every Flat Map Distorts Something
sections.body: A curved surface cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing it, and this is not a limitation of technique but a theorem. Carl Friedrich Gauss proved in 1827, in the result he named the Theorema Egregium or remarkable theorem, that the curvature of a surface is an intrinsic property that no bending can change. A sphere has positive curvature and a plane has none, so no mapping between them can preserve all distances. Every projection therefore distorts something, and the cartographer's task is choosing which distortions to accept. Projections are classified by what they do preserve. A conformal projection preserves angles and therefore local shapes: at any given point the scale is the same in every direction, although it varies from point to point. An equal area projection preserves the ratio of areas but must distort shape to do it. An equidistant projection keeps distances true from one or two chosen points, or along particular lines, but not everywhere. No projection can be both conformal and equal area. The nineteenth century French cartographer Nicolas Auguste Tissot devised a neat way of showing all of this, drawing small circles from the globe as they appear on the map: where they remain circles the projection is conformal, where they become ellipses of the same area it is equal area. Topographic series are almost always conformal, for reasons that are entirely practical. A bearing measured with a protractor on the sheet must correspond to a bearing walked on the ground, and a rectangular building must appear rectangular. Over the small area of one sheet the area distortion of a conformal projection is negligible, so nothing is lost by the choice. The workhorse is the Transverse Mercator. An ordinary Mercator projection, published by Gerardus Mercator in 1569, wraps a cylinder around the equator; the transverse version turns the cylinder ninety degrees so it touches along a chosen meridian instead. Johann Heinrich Lambert described it in 1772 and Gauss and Krüger later worked out the rigorous formulas for an ellipsoid, which is why it is often called Gauss Krüger. Its virtue is very low distortion close to that central meridian; its limitation is that distortion grows quickly with distance east or west of it, which is why it is always used in narrow north south strips. Countries wide in the east west direction instead use the Lambert Conformal Conic, which touches along one or two standard parallels, and this is why French national mapping uses Lambert zones and why aeronautical charts at one to five hundred thousand generally do too. The polar regions, where a meridian based system breaks down, use polar stereographic projections instead. The projection in use is always stated in the margin of a properly made sheet, and it is worth reading, because it tells you how the grid behaves and how far grid north will diverge from true north at your position.

sections.heading: Grids: UTM, MGRS and National Grid Systems
sections.body: Latitude and longitude are excellent for saying where something is on the planet and poor for measuring distances on a sheet of paper. A degree of latitude is a consistent 111 kilometres or so, but a degree of longitude shrinks from 111 kilometres at the equator to nothing at the poles, so the graticule is not a square grid and you cannot simply scale distances off it with a ruler. Topographic series therefore overprint a metric grid derived from the projection, in which coordinates are plain distances in metres and the squares really are squares. The Universal Transverse Mercator system is the most widespread. It divides the world into sixty zones, each six degrees of longitude wide, numbered one to sixty eastward starting at the antimeridian, so zone 31 begins at the Greenwich meridian. Each zone gets its own Transverse Mercator projection centred on its own middle meridian, which keeps distortion within about one part in a thousand, or a metre per kilometre, anywhere in the zone. That is achieved by setting the scale factor at the central meridian to 0.9996 rather than 1, deliberately shrinking the middle so the surface cuts the ellipsoid along two lines roughly 180 kilometres either side, where scale is exactly true. Coverage runs from 80 degrees south to 84 degrees north, split into latitude bands of eight degrees lettered C to X with I and O omitted to avoid confusion with digits; the polar caps use a separate stereographic system. A few zones are irregular: zone 32 is widened over southwest Norway and several are reshaped around Svalbard. Within a zone, coordinates are made positive by convention. The central meridian is assigned an easting of 500,000 metres, so real eastings run from roughly 166,000 to 834,000. Northings are measured from the equator in the northern hemisphere, while the southern hemisphere assigns the equator a value of 10,000,000 metres and counts down. The Military Grid Reference System repackages the same numbers into something speakable. A reference consists of the zone number, the band letter, a two letter code identifying a hundred kilometre square, and then equal numbers of easting and northing digits. The digit count sets the precision: two digits per axis gives ten kilometres, four gives one kilometre, six gives a hundred metres, eight gives ten metres and ten gives one metre. Many countries run their own equivalent. The British National Grid uses a Transverse Mercator centred on two degrees west with a false origin placed southwest of the country so all values are positive, and labels hundred kilometre squares with two letters, so a reference such as SU followed by three digits east and three north locates a point to a hundred metres. Whatever the system, the ordering rule never changes: eastings first, then northings.

sections.heading: How Sheets Are Bounded, Sized and Made to Join
sections.body: There are two ways to cut a country into sheets, and which one a series uses shapes almost everything about how it behaves in the hand. The first is to bound each sheet by lines of latitude and longitude, producing what is called a quadrangle. The second is to bound it by lines of the projected grid, producing a true rectangle in map coordinates. Quadrangle sheets have a subtlety that surprises people: they are not rectangles. Meridians converge toward the poles, so the north edge of a quadrangle is shorter than the south edge and the sheet is really a narrow trapezoid, usually squared off in printing. The convergence is substantial. One minute of longitude spans about 1,855 metres at the equator, about 1,421 metres at forty degrees north and only about 928 metres at sixty degrees north. A series with fixed angular sheet dimensions therefore covers far less ground per sheet at high latitude, which is why the United States Geological Survey used seven and a half minute quadrangles across the contiguous states but switched to wider angular sheets in Alaska to keep the printed area sensible. That American series is the classic example of the type. Each sheet spans seven and a half minutes of latitude by seven and a half of longitude at a scale of one to twenty four thousand, covering somewhere between about fifty and seventy square miles depending on latitude, and roughly fifty five thousand sheets were needed for the lower forty eight states. The programme ran for some five decades and was completed in 1992, which is a useful reminder of the sheer scale of the undertaking. Grid bounded series are tidier to use. Ordnance Survey Landranger sheets at one to fifty thousand are forty kilometre squares aligned to the National Grid, and two hundred and four of them cover Great Britain. Swiss national sheets at one to twenty five thousand each cover a neat 17.5 by 12 kilometres, with two hundred and forty seven sheets covering the country. Because the sheet edges follow grid lines, plotting a grid reference near an edge is straightforward. The problem every series shares is the edge itself. A route running along a sheet boundary requires two maps and a great deal of unfolding, and the most important terrain is often exactly where the cut fell. Some series print an overlap margin, some publish specially centred sheets covering popular areas that straddle a join, and several national agencies now sell custom maps centred wherever the buyer asks. When none of that is available, buying the neighbouring sheet is not optional. Check adjoining sheets before a trip rather than discovering the gap in the rain.

sections.heading: Sheet Numbering, Indexes and the International Map of the World
sections.body: Once a country is cut into thousands of pieces, the pieces need names, and there are two philosophies. Sequential numbering simply counts the sheets, so British Landranger sheets run from 1 in Shetland to 204 in the far southwest. This is easy to say and easy to order, but the number tells you nothing about where the sheet is; you need an index diagram to find out. Systematic numbering instead encodes position in the designation, so the code itself tells a trained reader roughly where on the planet the sheet falls and which codes lie to the north and east. The dominant systematic scheme descends from an ambitious international project.
