When only three satellites are visible, a receiver can still produce a degraded two-dimensional fix by substituting an assumed altitude for the missing equation: marine receivers may assume sea level, and aviation receivers can hold the last barometric altitude. This 2D mode keeps a position on the screen, but the fix inherits the full error of the altitude assumption — assume sea level while standing on a 1,000-meter plateau and the horizontal position can be dragged off by a comparable amount. Treat a 2D fix as a rough indication, not a position to run a bearing from, and expect a full three-dimensional solution only with four or more satellites usable above the horizon at once.

sections.heading: Atomic Clocks and the Relativity Correction
sections.body: GPS is one of the few consumer technologies whose engineering fails outright unless both of Einstein's theories of relativity are taken into account, and the arithmetic shows why. Radio waves travel about 30 centimeters per nanosecond, so a timing error of a single microsecond translates into roughly 300 meters of position error; keeping fixes good to a few meters demands clocks honest to a few nanoseconds over the hours between ground-control updates. That is why each satellite carries multiple cesium or rubidium atomic clocks, instruments that discipline their tick rate to the resonance frequency of atoms rather than to a vibrating crystal. Two relativistic effects then act on those clocks in opposite directions. Special relativity says a clock moving fast relative to an observer ticks slower: GPS satellites travel at roughly 14,000 kilometers per hour, about 3.9 kilometers per second, which slows their clocks by about 7 microseconds per day compared with clocks on the ground. General relativity says a clock deeper in a gravitational field ticks slower — equivalently, a clock higher up ticks faster: at 20,200 kilometers altitude the satellites sit in markedly weaker gravity than the surface, which speeds their clocks by about 45 microseconds per day. The two effects do not cancel. The gravitational speed-up dominates, leaving a net gain of roughly 38 microseconds per day relative to ground clocks. Multiply that out and the consequence is unmistakable: 38 microseconds at 300 meters per microsecond is on the order of 10 kilometers of accumulated position error per day — the system would be useless within hours. Engineers pre-compensate before launch by deliberately setting each satellite's clock frequency slightly low, at 10.22999999543 megahertz instead of the nominal 10.23 megahertz, so that once in orbit, relativity speeds it up to tick at exactly the intended rate as seen from the ground. The correction was designed in from the beginning, and cautiously: the 1977 experimental satellite that first carried this offset had it built behind a switch that could be left off, because some engineers doubted the relativistic prediction would appear at full magnitude in practice. In orbit, the clock drifted at almost precisely the predicted rate, the correction was switched on, and the mission doubled as one of the cleanest confirmations of general relativity ever performed. Small residual effects remain even after the factory offset — each orbit is slightly elliptical, so a satellite's speed and altitude vary around every revolution, and the navigation message includes a correction term the receiver applies for that eccentricity. The practical takeaway is a useful calibration for intuition: the blue dot on a phone works only because curved spacetime is accounted for, continuously, every second.

sections.heading: The Four GNSS Constellations: GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou
sections.body: GPS, operated by the United States Space Force, was the first fully global system, declared fully operational in 1995 with a baseline constellation of 24 satellites in six orbital planes about 20,200 kilometers up; the operational fleet usually runs above 30 so spares are always aloft. It is no longer alone. Russia's GLONASS reached global coverage in the mid-1990s, decayed with the post-Soviet economy, and was restored to full strength by 2011; its 24 satellites orbit slightly lower, near 19,100 kilometers, and its legacy signals use a different radio scheme — each satellite transmits on its own slightly offset frequency, where GPS satellites share one frequency and are distinguished by code. The European Union's Galileo, operational since 2016, was designed under civilian control from the outset, orbits near 23,200 kilometers, and offers one of the most precise open signals available along with an authenticated service designed to resist spoofing. China's BeiDou completed its third-generation global constellation in 2020 with a hybrid architecture: most satellites in medium Earth orbit like the others, plus geostationary and inclined geosynchronous satellites parked over the Asia-Pacific for dense regional coverage. Around these four global systems sit regional augmentations — Japan's QZSS flies highly inclined orbits engineered so a satellite is almost always nearly overhead in Japan, precisely to serve city streets where low satellites are blocked, and India's NavIC covers the subcontinent. Collectively they are the Global Navigation Satellite Systems, GNSS, and the plural matters in practice. Virtually every modern phone chipset and dedicated receiver tracks several constellations at once, so instead of the 6 to 10 usable satellites GPS alone provides, a device under open sky typically locks 20 to 30. The payoff is threefold: more satellites means better geometry and therefore better accuracy; more signals mean faster first fixes; and independence between systems means a fault or outage in one constellation does not blind the receiver. There is a frequency dimension as well. Newer satellites broadcast a second civilian signal near 1176 megahertz — L5 on GPS, E5 on Galileo — with a wider, more robust structure that resists reflected-signal errors better than the original L1 signal, and since 2018 flagship phones have shipped dual-frequency receivers that use both. Comparing the two frequencies also lets a receiver directly measure and remove the delay the ionosphere imposes on the signal, one of the larger residual error sources in single-frequency fixes. For the person holding the device the lesson is simple: a modern multi-constellation, dual-frequency receiver is meaningfully more accurate and far more robust in difficult terrain than the GPS-only units of a decade ago, and settings that enable all constellations should be left on.

sections.heading: Dilution of Precision: Why Accuracy Varies
sections.body: Two fixes made with the same receiver and the same number of satellites can differ in accuracy by an order of magnitude, and the reason is geometry rather than signal quality. Dilution of precision, or DOP, quantifies how the spatial arrangement of the satellites in use amplifies or suppresses the underlying ranging error. The intuition is the same as taking compass bearings on two landmarks: if the landmarks sit ninety degrees apart, the two bearing lines cross cleanly and your plotted position is crisp; if they sit five degrees apart, the lines cross at a shallow angle and a tiny bearing error slides the intersection a long way. Satellites spread widely across the sky — some high, some low, in different directions — intersect their range spheres at a sharp point and produce a low DOP; satellites clustered in one region of sky intersect at grazing angles and produce a high one. DOP works as a multiplier. The receiver's raw ranging accuracy — the combined effect of clock, orbit, atmospheric, and reflection errors — is scaled by the DOP value to give the expected position error: a receiver ranging to about 3 meters with an HDOP of 1.5 should deliver horizontal accuracy around 4 to 5 meters, while the same receiver in a slot canyon with an HDOP of 8 could be off by 25 meters with no warning beyond the number itself. Receivers report several flavors: HDOP for horizontal, VDOP for vertical, PDOP for the combined three-dimensional position, and GDOP folding in time. A common rule of thumb rates values below 2 as excellent, 2 to 5 as good and fully adequate for navigation, 5 to 10 as usable but degraded, and anything above 10 as suspect regardless of how many signal bars the screen shows. Vertical accuracy deserves its own caution. Every satellite a receiver uses is above the horizon — none can ever be observed from below — so the geometry constraining altitude is inherently one-sided and weaker than the geometry constraining horizontal position. VDOP typically runs one and a half to two times HDOP, which is why the altitude on a GPS screen commonly wanders by two or three times the horizontal error, and why serious elevation work leans on barometric altimeters calibrated at known points instead. Because satellite orbits are published weeks ahead, DOP is also predictable: surveyors routinely plan observation windows around hours of favorable geometry, and the same almanac data explains why a receiver in a ravine may deliver a poor fix at one hour and a solid one two hours later, once the constellation has rotated into a better arrangement overhead. Checking the accuracy or DOP figure before trusting a critical fix costs nothing and catches most bad-geometry readings.

sections.heading: Urban Canyons and Multipath Interference
sections.body: Walk down a street lined with tall buildings and watch a phone's blue dot leap across the street, into a lobby, or half a block away, and you are watching two distinct failure modes stack. The first is plain blockage: buildings hide most of the sky, cutting the visible satellites down to whatever narrow strip remains open overhead — often a line of satellites along the street's axis, which is precisely the clustered, high-DOP geometry that turns small ranging errors into large position errors, especially in the cross-street direction. The second and more insidious problem is multipath. Radio waves at GPS frequencies reflect efficiently off glass curtain walls, metallized window coatings, and steel cladding, so the signal reaching the antenna may have bounced once or several times on the way. Every bounce lengthens the path. Because the receiver converts travel time directly into distance, a reflected signal reads as a satellite farther away than it truly is, and the corrupted pseudorange drags the computed position with it. The worst case is non-line-of-sight reception: the direct signal is completely blocked and only a reflection arrives, so the measurement is wrong by the full length of the detour — routinely tens of meters, occasionally more than a hundred in glass-walled districts. Unlike random noise, multipath error is systematic and can persist as long as you stand in the same spot, so a stationary receiver may hold a confidently wrong position rather than scattering around the true one. Mitigations exist at every level of the industry. Survey-grade equipment uses choke-ring antennas and correlator designs that reject late-arriving copies of the signal; the newer L5-band signals were designed with a sharper structure that makes reflections easier to distinguish; and smartphone mapping software fuses satellite fixes with inertial sensors, WiFi, and map logic — some platforms even trace signals against 3D building models to correct predictable urban reflections, which is why the blue dot in a major city behaves noticeably better than raw satellite accuracy would suggest. A pedestrian can borrow the same reasoning without any of the hardware. Position fixes taken at intersections, plazas, or parks, where the open sky widens in more than one direction, are systematically better than fixes taken mid-block against a facade. Standing still for thirty seconds to a minute lets the filtering settle, and watching whether the dot stays put is a fast honesty check. Above all, calibrate skepticism to surroundings: the same handset that reliably delivers three-to-five-meter accuracy in open country should be assumed capable of twenty-meter errors between towers, and a dropped pin in a dense downtown — a meeting point, a parked car — deserves a cross-street or landmark noted alongside it rather than blind trust.

sections.heading: Canopy, Indoors, and Weak-Signal Environments
sections.body: GPS signals arrive at the ground almost unbelievably faint. A satellite's navigation payload transmits with roughly the power of a household light bulb — on the order of tens of watts — and that energy spreads across a footprint covering nearly half the planet from 20,200 kilometers away. By the time it reaches your antenna the received power is around a ten-quadrillionth of a watt, well below the thermal noise generated inside the receiver itself. The signal is recoverable at all only because of correlation: the receiver knows each satellite's code pattern in advance and multiplies the incoming noise against it, and thousands of code repetitions add up coherently while the noise averages toward zero, lifting the signal out of static the way a familiar voice emerges from a crowded room. That processing trick has limits, and obstructions find them. The L-band frequencies GNSS uses, near 1.5 gigahertz, are absorbed efficiently by water, and living vegetation is largely water: dense forest canopy attenuates and scatters the signal, wet canopy markedly more so, and under a rain-soaked stand of conifers a consumer receiver may hold only a degraded, wandering fix or lose lock outright. Indoors the situation is more severe again — masonry, concrete, and metal roofing attenuate far more than foliage, and most receivers cannot acquire a fix inside a typical building, though a high-sensitivity chip that already holds lock may cling to a weak solution near a window for a while. Slot canyons, caves, vehicle interiors, and even a body between antenna and sky all subtract from the margin. Two practical consequences follow. First, acquiring a fix is harder than keeping one: locking onto a satellite requires more signal than tracking it, so a receiver switched on under heavy canopy may fail where the same receiver, given a fix in a clearing first, would have carried it into the trees. Starting the device at a trailhead or opening with a clear view, and letting it settle before walking into cover, exploits this asymmetry. Second, degradation is gradual and often silent — the receiver keeps drawing a position dot even as its quality decays, so the reported accuracy estimate deserves a glance whenever the sky above is anything less than open. When a position genuinely matters under marginal conditions — a cache, a vehicle, a junction — improve the odds deliberately: move to the largest available break in the canopy, hold the device flat and away from your body with the sky exposed, give it a minute to settle, and use the averaging function many handhelds provide, which records dozens of fixes over several minutes and stores the mean. None of that makes a bad sky good, but it reliably turns a poor measurement into a fair one.

sections.heading: Jamming and Spoofing: When GPS Lies to You
sections.body: Jamming and spoofing are distinct threats, and the distinction determines both the symptoms and the defense. Jamming is brute-force denial. Because the genuine satellite signals arrive weaker than the receiver's own internal noise, drowning them out takes very little: a transmitter of modest power broadcasting noise on the GNSS frequencies can deny reception for hundreds of meters around it, and larger military systems for far greater ranges. Cheap illegal jammers, often bought to defeat fleet-tracking devices, have caused repeatedly documented collateral disruption — the best-known case being a delivery driver whose dashboard jammer intermittently disrupted a GPS-based landing aid at Newark airport as he drove past on the adjacent highway. A jammed receiver, at least, fails honestly: the fix disappears, accuracy estimates collapse, or the position freezes at the last known point, and the user knows something is wrong. Spoofing is the more dangerous failure because it is deceptive rather than disruptive. A spoofer broadcasts counterfeit signals imitating real satellites, typically slightly stronger than the genuine ones so the receiver's tracking loops latch onto the forgery, and then feeds timing that walks the computed position wherever the attacker chooses. The receiver reports normal signal strength, plausible satellite counts, and a confident fix that is simply false. Documented incidents have moved from curiosity to routine: ships in the Black Sea reporting positions clustered at an inland airport kilometers from the sea, systematic false positioning around protected sites, and, since the early 2020s, frequent spoofing of airliners near active conflict zones, with navigation systems abruptly reporting impossible jumps, wrong airports, or clock errors that cascade into other aircraft systems. Detection is hardest for exactly the systems that trust satellite navigation most, which is why aviation and shipping increasingly cross-check fixes against inertial navigation — accelerometers and gyroscopes that no radio signal can touch — and why Galileo now offers an authenticated open signal, OSNMA, that lets a receiver cryptographically verify the navigation data it decodes. For an individual with a phone or handheld, the realistic posture is awareness rather than countermeasures. Near conflict zones, contested borders, ports, and military exercises, treat satellite positioning as suspect. The warning signs are recognizable: a position that jumps implausibly, indicated speed wildly different from your actual movement, a device clock that suddenly disagrees with local time, or a fix that flatly contradicts terrain you can see. Any of these is a prompt to fall back on the independent references that spoofing cannot touch — the map, the compass bearing, the landmark on the horizon — and to treat the reappearance of a clean-looking fix with suspicion until it has agreed with the visible world for a while. A confident screen is not evidence; agreement with reality is.

sections.heading: How Your Phone Gets a Fix So Fast: Assisted GPS
sections.body: A receiver switched on completely cold — no idea of time, position, or which satellites are overhead — faces a slow bootstrap. Everything it needs is broadcast by the satellites themselves in the navigation message, but that message trickles down at just 50 bits per second, orders of magnitude slower than even a 1980s modem. Each satellite's precise orbital data, the ephemeris, takes about 30 seconds to transmit and must be received without interruption; the almanac describing the whole constellation's coarse orbits takes a full 12.5 minutes to cycle. That is why an old dedicated unit, or a phone in a radio-silent wilderness, can take from half a minute to several minutes to produce its first fix, and why receiver start-ups are classed as cold, warm, or hot depending on how much of that data is already in memory and still valid — ephemeris data expires after roughly four hours, while the almanac stays useful for weeks. Assisted GPS, or A-GPS, short-circuits the bootstrap. When a phone has any data connection, it fetches current ephemeris and almanac data from network servers in a fraction of a second instead of waiting on the 50-bit-per-second broadcast, and it seeds its position estimate from cell-tower identity and nearby WiFi access points, whose locations are held in vast crowdsourced databases. Knowing roughly where it is, what time it is, and which satellites should be overhead, the chip can search a tiny slice of the timing-and-frequency space instead of all of it, lock weak signals it would otherwise have missed, and deliver a fix within seconds — the dramatic improvement in time-to-first-fix that makes a phone feel instant. Many devices extend the idea with predicted ephemeris, downloading days of projected orbits in advance so that fast fixes survive periods with no connectivity. Two practical points follow for field use. First, the assistance requires a network, but the positioning does not: a GPS receiver is purely passive, listening only, and works perfectly in airplane mode. The efficient pattern for a backcountry trip is to open the mapping app and get a solid fix while still in coverage — loading assistance data and fresh ephemeris — then switch to airplane mode, which preserves full satellite function while stopping the battery-draining hunt for absent cell service. Second, understand what the fallback looks like: with satellites unavailable, a phone can still estimate position purely from cell towers and WiFi, typically to within tens or hundreds of meters in town, which is why a phone deep inside a shopping center still shows a plausible dot. In terrain with no towers and no mapped WiFi that fallback vanishes entirely, and the difference between a satellite fix and a network guess — invisible in the city — becomes the difference between a position and nothing.

sections.heading: Waypoints, Tracks, and Routes: The Units of Digital Navigation
sections.body: Every digital navigation tool, from a rugged handheld to a phone hiking app, organizes position data around three building blocks, and using them well means understanding what each one is for. A waypoint is a single stored coordinate marking one place — the parked car, a spring, a campsite, a trail junction — the digital equivalent of circling a spot on a paper map, usually with a name and symbol attached. A track, or breadcrumb trail, is a passively recorded sequence of fixes the device logs automatically as you move, one point every few seconds or meters, forming a continuous record of where you have actually been; from it the software can later reconstruct distance traveled, moving time, and the elevation profile. A route is the planned counterpart: an ordered list of waypoints you intend to visit in sequence, with the device computing the bearing and distance of each leg, or, in road navigation, computing a suggested path along mapped roads between them. The track-versus-route distinction is the one that bites in the field, because they answer different questions — a track says where you went, a route says where you mean to go — and devices store and navigate them differently. Confusing them produces the classic frustration of trying to 'navigate to' a thousand-point track and getting nonsense. Most devices bridge the gap with a back-track or reverse-track function that converts the recorded trail into a navigable path home, which is among the most genuinely lifesaving features in the toolset: a track recorded on the walk in can be followed back out through fog, darkness, or featureless terrain with a fidelity no memory can match. That only works if recording was on, so make starting the track log at the trailhead as habitual as locking the car. A few disciplines keep the system trustworthy. Name waypoints as you create them — 'CAR', 'SPRING2', 'JCT-N' — because a list of twenty auto-numbered entries is worthless under stress. Check the track-log settings once: the logging interval trades detail against memory and battery, and a device set to log by large distance steps will round off switchbacks. Plan routes at home on a large screen where mistakes are cheap, then transfer them; all mainstream tools exchange waypoints, tracks, and routes through the GPX file format, an open standard that moves data between apps and devices without loss. And when following a route, remember what the device is actually doing: unless it is road-routing, the arrow points along a straight line to the next waypoint, cheerfully through the lake or over the cliff between you and it — legs must be planned, and walked, with the terrain in mind.

sections.heading: Datums and WGS84: Why Coordinate Systems Must Match
sections.body: Earth is not a perfect sphere: it bulges at the equator, and its gravity field is lumpy, so any coordinate system must be anchored to a mathematical model of the planet's shape — a datum — that defines exactly where latitude zero, longitude zero, and the reference surface itself sit. Change the datum and every coordinate on the map shifts, even though the ground does not. Modern satellite navigation effectively settled the question worldwide: virtually all devices, phone apps, and current digital maps use WGS84, the World Geodetic System 1984, a global ellipsoid model maintained by the United States government specifically to support satellite positioning. The trap lives in older material. Paper topographic maps drafted before the 1990s were commonly built on regional datums tuned for local fit — NAD27 across North America, and dozens of national datums elsewhere — and their coordinates disagree with WGS84 by amounts that vary with location: commonly tens of meters, over two hundred meters in parts of North America, and several hundred meters against some older datums abroad. The danger is silent, because coordinates are just numbers. A latitude-longitude pair read from a WGS84 device and plotted on a NAD27 map lands on a real, plausible-looking spot that is simply the wrong spot, with nothing on either screen or paper to flag the mismatch. The defense is procedural: every quality paper map states its datum in the margin, every serious GPS device and app has a datum setting, and the two must match before any coordinate crosses between them — with WGS84 as the default whenever there is doubt. A related and equally silent hazard is coordinate format. The same point can be written as decimal degrees, degrees-minutes-seconds, degrees and decimal minutes, or a UTM grid reference, and misreading one format as another produces errors of kilometers; when passing coordinates to anyone — especially rescue services — state the format and datum explicitly and have the numbers read back. Altitude carries its own datum subtlety. A GNSS receiver natively measures height above the WGS84 ellipsoid, the smooth mathematical surface, but 'elevation' on maps means height above mean sea level, and the two differ by up to about a hundred meters depending on where on Earth you stand, because sea level follows the lumpy gravity field rather than the smooth ellipsoid. Receivers correct for this internally with a stored geoid model, which is why the displayed elevation usually matches the map — but a raw ellipsoidal height from survey equipment or a data feed will not, and that discrepancy has confused more than one user comparing numbers. The single habit that prevents this whole class of error: whenever a coordinate moves between two systems — device to map, app to app, voice to radio — confirm datum and format at both ends first.

sections.heading: Building a Digital Navigation Field Kit
sections.body: Reliable digital navigation in the field is a systems problem, not a gadget purchase: batteries die, screens crack in falls, cold saps charge, and signal is never guaranteed, so the kit below treats the electronics as one redundant layer among several rather than the whole plan. The battery items deserve the most forethought, because power is the one failure mode you can actually manage. A phone's screen and its cellular radio are the two dominant drains, and in the backcountry the radio is the worse offender — a phone with no coverage burns charge relentlessly hunting for towers, which is why switching to airplane mode with GPS still active can stretch a day of battery into several. A 10,000 milliamp-hour power bank refills a typical phone roughly twice; carry the correct cable, and keep both bank and phone warm in cold weather, since lithium cells deliver sharply less capacity near and below freezing — an inside pocket is worth hours of runtime. The offline maps matter equally: download tiles for the whole area, at high zoom levels, while still on WiFi, and open them once before leaving coverage to confirm they actually render. The paper map and compass are not nostalgia; they are the only layer immune to every electronic failure at once, and they earn their place only if the map's datum matches the device and you have practiced with them recently. The written waypoint list is the cheapest insurance in the kit — coordinates on paper survive anything that kills the electronics, and let you re-enter critical points into a borrowed or replacement device. Assemble and test everything at home before the trip: charge the bank, verify the cable actually charges the device, load and open the maps, and mark a test waypoint, because a kit that has never been exercised is a list of assumptions, not a plan.
ingredients: A GPS-capable smartphone or dedicated handheld GPS unit with offline map tiles for your area downloaded in advance
A portable battery pack or power bank, fully charged, with the correct charging cable
The device set to airplane mode or GPS-only mode in the field to conserve battery, since cellular searching drains power fast with no signal
A physical paper topographic map of the area, printed or waterproofed, using the same datum as your GPS device
A baseplate compass and the working knowledge to use it with the map
A written or printed list of key waypoint coordinates (trailhead, campsite, water sources, bailout points) as a backup in case the device is lost or fails
Spare batteries if your device uses replaceable batteries rather than a sealed rechargeable cell
A small notebook and pencil to log position and time manually at intervals, as a low-tech track log

sections.heading: How to Mark and Navigate Back to a Waypoint
sections.body: Marking your position and navigating back to it later is the single most immediately valuable GPS skill, and it earns that rank in practice: people fail to relocate a parked vehicle, a camp, or the point where they left a trail far more often than they fail to walk a straight line. Two pieces of context make the procedure below work better. First, accuracy: a consumer receiver under open sky typically fixes within about three to five meters, so a saved waypoint will bring you to the right clearing but not necessarily to a small object. Mark small targets — a cache under one particular tree, gear stashed off-trail — with a written note or a photo of the surroundings in addition to the coordinates, and consider the waypoint-averaging function many handhelds offer, which refines an important waypoint by averaging fixes over several minutes. Second, geometry: the 'Go To' function draws a straight line from you to the target, and the pointer will indicate that line regardless of what lies along it — water, cliffs, deadfall — so returning is a repeated cycle of following the bearing where the terrain allows and detouring where it does not, letting the arrow re-converge after each detour rather than fighting to hold the line. Practice the full cycle somewhere consequence-free first; a town park teaches the menus in ten minutes, and that is exactly the fluency you want to already have before dusk, fatigue, and weather are attached to the problem.
steps: Stand still at the exact location you want to save and let the device settle onto a stable fix, ideally with a low DOP reading and several satellites locked, before proceeding.
Open the device's Mark Waypoint function, usually a dedicated button on handheld units or a menu option labeled 'Save Location' or 'Drop Pin' on phone apps.
Give the waypoint a short, memorable name or number, such as 'CAR' or 'CAMP1', rather than accepting an anonymous default label, since you may save many waypoints over a trip.
Confirm the save and verify the waypoint now appears in the device's waypoint list with reasonable coordinates.
When you are ready to return, open the waypoint list, select the saved point, and choose the 'Go To' or 'Navigate' function.
Follow the on-screen bearing and distance readout, which continuously updates as you move, keeping the directional arrow or compass needle pointed straight ahead.

Periodically cross-check the device's suggested direction against visible terrain features and, if carrying one, a physical compass bearing, rather than following the screen blindly through terrain you can see is wrong.

Upon arrival, the distance readout will approach zero; stop and visually confirm you have reached the intended feature, since GPS accuracy of a few meters can still place you slightly off from a small target.

sections.heading: GPS as a Tool, Not a Replacement for Map and Compass
sections.body: Every capability described in this guide comes with the same honest caveat: a GPS receiver is a battery-powered electronic device, and every such device eventually fails. The failure catalog is mundane and comprehensive — a battery dead sooner than expected, a screen cracked in a fall, water past a worn seal, cold weather cutting lithium capacity, a device dropped down a slope — and to it must be added the failures no care can prevent: canopy or canyon blocking signal, poor satellite geometry, interference, or software that freezes at the worst moment. None of that makes satellite navigation unreliable in the sense that matters. As a primary tool for knowing precisely where you are, tracking elevation, and retracing a route, it is dramatically more accurate and less effortful than any traditional method, and refusing to use it well is its own kind of error. The failure that actually hurts people is cognitive rather than electronic: trusting the screen over the world. Search-and-rescue literature has a name for the pattern — 'death by GPS' — describing incidents where drivers and hikers followed routing onto impassable roads, into deserts, or past obvious cues that the environment was contradicting the device, because a confident interface invites the quiet surrender of judgment. The related, slower cost is skill atrophy: navigation by map and terrain is a perishable ability, and a season of pure screen-following erodes exactly the competence you will need on the day the screen goes dark. The remedies are habits, not hardware. Carry the paper map and compass, and use them enough — before the trip and during it — that they remain a genuine capability rather than a talisman in the pack. While navigating digitally, keep a running mental plot: glance from screen to landscape and back, name the ridge and the drainage you can see, and note roughly where you are on the paper map at natural pauses, so that a device failure demotes you to a slower method instead of to lost. Treat disagreement as information — when the arrow points somewhere the terrain says is wrong, stop and resolve the conflict with independent evidence rather than picking a side on faith. Tell someone your route and return time regardless of how much technology you carry, because the best navigation outcome of all is a short search. The professional model is the right one: a pilot uses the autopilot constantly, monitors it continuously, and stays ready to fly by hand without ceremony. Use GPS the same way — actively, gratefully, and never blindly — and let redundancy, not any single device, be the thing that keeps you found.

guides.safetyNote: GPS devices can fail, lose signal, or be spoofed by false signals — always carry a physical map and compass as backup and know how to navigate with them before you need to rely on that skill.
